title: Third field report: the remedy the product prescribes and refuses in the same breath
description: A third live report, and its sharpest item is one the plugin says to itself. At sign-off, _invariants.manifest_revalidated prints as its own repair: 'by sign-off it has to be settled - run /audit:task scope <id> --files ... to re-derive the index'. Every id it can name is done by then, and scope refused every done task - so the product hands you a command it refuses in the same breath. A live run spent 172,417 tokens on three fix-run subagents before finding that out. F271 widened the STARTED rule this week and left the SETTLED one, which is exactly the half that bites at sign-off. Analysis also found it is worse than reported: during sign-off the plan gate is at deny with ZERO covered files, because in_progress_task_map reads only in_progress tasks and every task is done by then - so a finding inside a task's files would not have helped either. The remaining items are a shell-fragile description that silently dropped the decisive clause of a brief, a commit verb that cannot converge and only explains itself on the second run, a write-guard that flags the plugin's own CLI writers because they file no claim, and a phase title that nothing can rename though a branch name derives from it.
desiredOutcome: No remedy this product prescribes is refused by the product at the moment it prescribes it; a brief cannot lose its decisive clause in silence; and the surfaces that warn about their own sanctioned writes say which writer they mean.

findings: P31.7 shipped half of its own declared outcome: `retarget --rename` moved the title in the shard and left the index STUB carrying the old one, which is exactly the storage wrinkle the task description names. Found by building a sharded fixture the first live drive had not; fixed inside the task (the file was already in its `files`), with rn3 and rn5 proving both directions - the refresh, and that a write moving no stub key still leaves the index alone, which is what lets two phase branches merge cleanly.

P31.6 was implemented WIDER than its declared `files`, and rightly: the reported writer was one of seven CLI-reachable journal writers that filed no claim, including `audit-journal.py append`, which the guard's own notice cites as a legitimate writer. The scope was settled afterwards through `/audit:task scope` on the done task - the F283 route this same phase restored - which is also how F294 was found.

Three agent reports contained claims I could not take at face value and re-derived: P31.4's corpus figures (mine differ, the verdict does not), P31.5's byte-identity of ONLY_THE_TRAIL (checked against HEAD), and every red-first table (re-run in the primary tree rather than read).

Recorded rather than fixed here, each with a measurement: F291 (the explorer's return contract is written in two files and nothing compares them), F292 (PLUGIN-BUILD-GUIDE.md still describes the pre-F268 commit spelling), F293 (--reason and --outcome carry the same shell risk as --description, and an unquoted heredoc still slips past the new guard), F294 (`files ⊇ tests.add` copies SENTENCES into a task's scope: 8 already in the plan, 94 more one call away), F295 (25 of 50 sampled (verb, flag) pairs on audit-task.py are accepted and silently ignored).

summary: Eight findings from a third live report, and the one that named the phase was the product prescribing a remedy it refuses in the same breath: at sign-off `manifest_revalidated` tells you to run `/audit:task scope <id>` on ids that are all `done`, and the verb exited 2 on every one of them. `scope` now splits TERMINAL - `cancelled` refused, `done` accepting an append-only widening, because growing a list can only relax a scope and the fileIndex re-derivation IS the settlement being asked for. Around it: a phase can be renamed and the rename reaches the branch slug it feeds and the index stub that duplicates it, refused once a branch is cut because three readers would then give two answers; a brief the shell has eaten is refused off argv and has a stdin route that cannot be eaten; the run that leaves the journal dirty is the run that explains it; the plugin's own CLI scripts file a write claim, so the guard stops flagging the plugin and still flags everything else; `/audit:init` asks what shares a file's data path; commands that ask for their output printed say WHERE; and the subagent refusal stops promising a widening sign-off cannot deliver. Verified live rather than by reading, in throwaway projects and a real git repository, with every new case proven red-first in both directions. Five further faults were found along the way and recorded rather than folded in.

tasks.title: F283: a done task's scope may still settle its index, and the sign-off route is documented
tasks.description: scope refused _mio.TERMINAL whole. Split it: cancelled stays refused, because nothing will be committed against it so there is no pairing to settle and no run a wider list could describe. done accepts an append-only widening, and the reasons were checked in the code rather than argued - commit_scope reads task.files LIVE and reports staged paths outside it, so growing the list can only move a path INTO allowed and never the reverse; and the fileIndex re-derivation the write performs is exactly the settlement manifest_revalidated asks for. The honest objection that remains is about the record rather than any verdict, so the journal row dates which attempt it grew during and the report says plainly that this settles the index rather than recording new work. Separately, orchestrator.md's Phase sign-off step 1 now names the route for a finding in a file no task declares - a NEW task, before anything is spawned - because that is new work needing its own commit, gate run and evidence row, and because the measured cost of not saying so was three refused subagents.

add: test_audit_task.py: a done task accepts an append-only widening and its report says the settlement is not new work
test_audit_task.py: a cancelled task still refuses, and the refusal says why the two differ
test_audit_task.py: the remedy manifest_revalidated prints at sign-off is one scope actually accepts

outcome.technical: scope splits TERMINAL: cancelled refused, done accepts an append-only widening. Six cases (sc4, wd10, st1-st5), each proven red by a mutation that moves its own claim - including st5, which reads the remedy out of _invariants' source and asserts the verb accepts it, so the two cannot drift apart again.

render_target_drift pins one literal across the seven docs whose output is the deliverable, following _areas.rule_drift rather than repeating a rule in a dozen files. rt1/rt2 proven red; rows in both prove-gates tables.

tasks.title: F290: a command that asks for its output printed says WHERE
tasks.description: commands/status.md said 'Print its stdout verbatim', and a live run read that as discharged - the Bash tool had run and its stdout WAS printed, to the tool result, so the reply said 'the report above' and the operator saw nothing. In Claude Code a tool result is collapsed behind the tool call. Nothing anywhere in the plugin says tool output is invisible to the user, and the same phrasing sits in a dozen command docs. Rather than repeating a rule in twelve files - one copy and eleven lies by this repository's own reckoning - one literal is pinned across the docs whose OUTPUT is the deliverable, following _areas.rule_drift's pattern for exactly this shape. Scoped to a named set because `verbatim` also describes text going INTO a manifest, and a rule that fired there would ask a bug report to explain the terminal.

add: test__refs.py: a doc telling you to print output verbatim without saying where is a finding, both directions

outcome.technical: The subagent refusal named both routes. Nothing had pinned the promise text, which is why it could be false for five weeks; h4b2 pins it now and goes red on the flat form.

tasks.title: F284: the refusal stops promising a widening the orchestrator may not have
tasks.description: require-plan tells a refused subagent 'It will widen the scope and tell you to carry on'. Measured, that is false at sign-off: in_progress_task_map reads only in_progress tasks, every task is done by then, so NO file is covered and the gate is at deny because phase.status is still in_progress. F283's widening settles an index and does not unblock an edit, so the honest instruction depends on where the run is: mid-flight the orchestrator widens, at sign-off it adds a task. The refusal must say which rather than promise one.

add: test_require_plan.py: the subagent refusal names both routes rather than promising a widening that may not exist

outcome.technical: shell_eaten_gap() reads five residue positions a shell leaves when it eats part of an argument; resolve_description() runs in main() before dispatch and before the lock, so a refused call costs no lock, no journal row and no rollback - and it covers all FOUR write sites, including retarget, which the brief did not name. --description - reads the brief off stdin in the dialect check-ado-item.py already uses, dropping only trailing newlines. Re-derived on my own corpus: 0 hits over 152 description strings and 0 over 606 adjacent prose strings, while the damaged brief is caught and `git fetch . b:p` is not. Nine cases (eb1-eb9), each proven red by a mutation moving its own claim; eb1 and the stdin boundary re-proven in the primary tree, and the whole thing driven live in zsh.
outcome.descriptive: A brief that reached the manifest missing exactly the clause its author thought worth quoting is now refused instead of written, and the refusal points at the route no shell can damage. The refusal is affordable because the way past it is the better input path, not a re-worded brief.

tasks.title: F285: a brief cannot lose its decisive clause in silence
tasks.description: Backticks in --description were consumed by the shell before audit-task.py saw them; the stored brief lost the condition that was its most important fact, and the script accepted and wrote it. Two things were measured over the 129 real description strings in this plan: space-before-comma catches the reported damage at ZERO false positives, and the intuitive unbalanced-backtick check is REFUTED - the shell removes both delimiters so the count stays even. The input repair follows the dialect that exists: five ADO scripts already take a path with '-' meaning stdin, and there is no --*-file flag anywhere in the plugin.

add: test_audit_task.py: a description carrying a shell-eaten gap is reported, and an ordinary sentence is not
test_audit_task.py: --description - reads the brief from stdin, so backticks never meet a shell

outcome.technical: _scoped_commit.render's success path prints TRAIL_ROW_WRITTEN, gated on `journalled` so it is a pair and never a default. The shared fact - a row names the SHA, so it lands outside the commit - is one constant, _scoped_commit.RIDES_ALONG, composed by both the notice and commit-audit-state.ONLY_THE_TRAIL; that refusal renders byte-identically to HEAD, checked rather than asserted. Placed in the shared renderer because commit-manifest-index.py has the same property (the journal is not on its allow-list), so the line is a lie in neither. cas27/cas28/cas29 added; cas27 and cas29 re-proven red-first in the primary tree. 30/30, 10/10, 18/18.
outcome.descriptive: The run that leaves the journal dirty is now the run that says so. It used to take a second run on a clean tree to learn why a tree just reported as committed had a modified file in it.

tasks.title: F286: the trailing journal row is explained on the run that creates it
tasks.description: The audit.state.committed row names the SHA, so it is appended after the commit and can never be inside it. That is inherent. The explanation exists and is well written - the module docstring says it at length, and a purpose-built sentence fires on a second run - but the run that CREATES the condition prints the SHA, the staged paths, and nothing about the row just written. So the operator meets a dirty tree first and the explanation second, which is one run too late.

add: test_commit_audit_state.py: the successful run says the trail row it just wrote rides along with the next commit

outcome.technical: _journal_io.append_from_cli() appends and files the claim under one fixed writer key, CLI_JOURNAL_WRITER = 'cli', mirrored in guard-bash-writes as CLI_WRITER because a hook may not import scripts/; _plugin_wrote now reads (sid, PANEL_WRITER, CLI_WRITER). The config is resolved once and handed to both halves, because the claim's slot is stateDir-relative and two loads could file it where the guard is not looking. Deliberately NOT a path exemption: exempting the journal directory would delete the guard, and mutating it that way goes red across six cases. Seven CLI writers converted, derived by an AST walk for append calls with two or more arguments rather than by search. pw6 states the rule - every journal append under scripts/ claims or goes red by name - so the eighth writer cannot arrive silently.
outcome.descriptive: Running the plugin's own commands from a shell no longer makes the next command draw a warning about the plugin's own write. The guard still speaks for a journal write nobody claimed, which is the write it exists for - driven live in a real repository, both directions.

tasks.title: F287: the plugin's own CLI writers file a claim, so the guard stops flagging them
tasks.description: After commit-audit-state.py ran, guard-bash-writes warned that a shell command wrote into the append-only journal; audit-journal.py verify then reported the chain clean. The guard already has a sanctioned-writer notion and it is deliberately NOT a path exemption - it reads per-writer claim sidecars, and its own recorded reasoning says honouring another session's claim would let real tampering pass. The gap is that _journal_io.record_plugin_write is a general API no CLI script calls: only journal-writes.py (session key) and _panel_write.py (the 'panel' key) file claims. Two constraints on the repair: a CLI invoked from Bash has no session id in argv so it needs a fixed writer key the way the panel has one, and _plugin_wrote iterates a hard-coded key tuple while guard-bash-writes may not import scripts/ - so the constant must be mirrored and pinned by a test exactly as PANEL_WRITER is. Separately the notice's own disambiguation list offers 'a panel save, or an edit and a shell command in one message' and does not name 'a plugin script you ran via Bash', which is the case that actually fired.

add: test_guard_bash_writes.py: a journal write a plugin CLI claimed is not flagged, and one nothing claimed still is
test__journal_io.py: the writer key the hook mirrors is the one the scripts file under

outcome.technical: retarget --rename TITLE writes phase.title through the same lock, revalidate-or-roll-back and journal row as every other manifest mutation. --rename and not --title: the verb's positional slot is already called title and carries the phase id. Refused once phase.branch is recorded, because resolve-branch.py:111 composes the branch from the title unconditionally while close-phase.py:133 and manage-worktrees.py:134 prefer the recorded name - three readers, two answers. THE SHARDED HALF WAS NOT FREE, which the phase review caught: _write_add rewrites the index only when the fileIndex moved, so the shard took the new title and the index stub kept the old one; _STUB_KEYS are now compared against the body and the index is dirtied only when one actually moved, which keeps the property that a phase RUN touches no index. rn1-rn5, every one proven red-first in both directions, and driven live on throwaway projects in both layouts.
outcome.descriptive: A phase whose scope widened can be given a title that describes it - while it is still waiting - and the rename reaches every place the title is stored, not only the one the reader happens to load. After the branch is cut the title is the record of what the branch was cut for, and the verb says so instead of silently disagreeing with itself.

tasks.title: F288: a phase can be renamed, and the rename reaches everything the title feeds
tasks.description: /audit:phase retarget takes --gate/--area/--outcome/--description and no --title, and phase.title is written at creation and never again - the panel does not touch it. So a phase whose scope widened keeps a title describing half of it. A rename is NOT cosmetic and that is why it needs a verb: _branch.slugify's docstring is literally 'phase.title -> the {slug} segment', consumed into '<prefix>/{phase}-{slug}'; sync.md maps phase to '[<phaseId>] <title>' and pushes on the next sync; and five render sites read it. Plus a storage wrinkle that settles verb-versus-hand-edit: under the sharded layout title is duplicated into the index stub and merged back with the body winning, so a hand rename touching only the shard leaves the stub stale. The branch consequence needs a decision rather than a default - a phase already on a branch must not silently resolve to a different one.

add: test_audit_task.py: retarget --title rewrites the shard AND the index stub, and refuses when the phase is already on a branch the title would move

outcome.technical: audit-explorer.md gained a coupling rule and a coupledPaths field shaped {path, shared}; the `shared` key forces the explorer to name the store, wire shape or generated type both sides touch, and [] is required so looked-and-found-none is not did-not-look. init.md restates the contract for its documented fallback path and carries the sibling paragraph to F272's at the bullet where `files` is populated, with the both-directions rule: a coupled path the fix would leave wrong is this task's work, and a task that claims its whole data path has the codebase as its scope. audit-reviewer.md narrows preExisting to what the change inherited. No analyser, no Python.
outcome.descriptive: The plan now asks what else is on a file's data path, which is where two of three findings in a live phase came from. It asks for the name of the thing shared, so the answer is checkable rather than a feeling of relatedness.

tasks.title: F289: /audit:init asks what shares a file's data path, not only what a task reads
tasks.description: Two of three review findings in one live phase were the same shape - a sibling component sharing a data path that no task's files covered. The reporter calls it a plan-authoring gap and the code agrees: init.md has no coupling vocabulary at all, files is populated straight from 'files from the finding', and the explorer's return contract is a flat per-finding list with no field for what else is on that data path. The precedent for the repair is already in the file and stops one noun short: 'Say what the task will create, not only what it will read' was added this week for F272. Its missing sibling is 'say what shares this file's data path'. This is prose plus a contract field, not a static analysis - nothing here should pretend to compute coupling in an audited codebase.
